replying_to: Replying to MutexMatch: Semi-supervised Learning with Mutex-based Consistency Regularization
display_title: Official Review of Paper957 by Reviewer y2Kv

content.summary_of_the_paper:
### New SSL algorithm that exploits mutual exclusions.

This paper proposed a novel semi-supervised algorithm that makes use of unlabeled examples that fall below the confidence threshold to additionally guide the network to learn *what it is not*, in addition to learning *what it is* using standard Fix-Match style. Overall, the method is simple and seems effective with little to no additional cost during training and testing. Extensive experiments provide meaningful insights into the model.
content.main_review:
### Strengths

- The paper is well written and the experiments are useful. 
- The idea to use the often-ignored lesser confident samples from the unlabeled set is novel and well motivated. 
- The overall framework using a true-negative classifier seems pretty general and easily adoptable to any existing approaches, although the proposed approach achieves SOTA using a FixMatch backbone. 

### Weaknesses

- I did not get the logic behind enforcing consistency regularization against TNC's predictions. While TPC consistency means that weak and strong augmentation predictions match, similar logic doesn't hold for TNC prediction. For example, the same horse image can *not* belong to a dog class as well as *not* belong to a zebra class. Isn't this opposite to enforcing consistency?
- From the Table 1, the numbers seem pretty strong. However, the variance of the reported accuracies for CIFAR-10 with 10 labels is very high. Although the absolute difference is ~10%, the variance is also ~10%, which requires further explanation.
- Similarly, on CIFAR-10 with 40 and 80 labels as well as CIFAR-100 with 200 labels, the difference of accuracy between next best method (CoMatch) and MutexMatch is marginal (93% vs 93.4%, 94% vs 94.3%) and often equivalent to the reported variance (0.2% and 0.8%). (It is completely fine with me if your method is not SOTA, but the high variance requires some explanation).
- Figure 9 is not present in sec 5.2. Did you mean Fig 7?
- From fig 7a,b,c, it seems that the difference between various ways of training TNC give roughly the same result. So the take-home message of this whole ablation seems pretty weak to me.
- From fig 7c, the complementary pseudo label accuracy seems low for Rev-Norm while the overall accuracy in fig 7a seems almost equal. This raises the question if the complementary accuracy and original accuracy have any correlation at all on this dataset?
- Can the authors provide an ablation into the effectiveness of losses Lp and Ln from eq 1? By not using one or both of lambda_p and lambda_n, what would be the drop in performance? The ablation provided in Fig 9 in the supplementary seems odd to me. lambda_n is varies between 1-20 while lambda_sep is varies between 0.25-1.00, although the losses seem to be roughly of the same scale. A better ablation of the hyperparameters is needed to really distill the effectiveness of the proposed losses.
- It is not really clear what happens at test-time. Do we simply drop the TNC classifier and predict using the TPC network?
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposed a novel technique for semi-supervised learning by effectively using the low-confident unlabeled samples. The overall framework is simple and well-motivated but few concerns regarding the analysis into the approach remain, which are mentioned above. Nevertheless, the method seems effective for SSL and and if the authors could clarify the questions raised, I would be happy to update the score. 

Post rebuttal 
-------------------------
I appreciate the authors' efforts in addressing all the queries raised. While I feel this work has an interesting and technically novel motivation, I also think it requires further analysis, ablations and insights to match the intuition presented. Therefore, I am inclined to keep my score but would not argue if the paper gets accepted.

content.title: Response to reviewer y2Kv (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful reading and detailed feedback on our work！ We sincerely believe that your comments have value and are of great benefit to our work. In response to your question, we will give the reply below.

>Q1. I did not get the logic behind enforcing consistency regularization against TNC's predictions. While TPC consistency means that weak and strong augmentation predictions match, similar logic doesn't hold for TNC prediction. For example, the same horse image can not belong to a dog class as well as not belong to a zebra class. Isn't this opposite to enforcing consistency?

We feel sorry if our mentioning consistency regularization on TNC causes any confusion. 
- We think that it is reasonable to use consistency regularization on TNC at the sample level, because we only need TNC to show the exclusion function of various classes at the dataset level, which is shown in Section 4.3. e.g., for a horse image denoted $h_{1}$, we enforce consistency regularization on TNC indicating $h_{1}$ don't belong to a dog class, TNC can outputs other complementary labels (e.g., don't belong to a zebra class) for another horse image denoted $h_{2}$ at the same time. For the set of horse images $H=(h_{1},...,h_{n})$, TNC outputs various complementary labels for $h_{i} \in H$ when consistency regularization are enforced on it, which shown in Fig. 4. Although we don't use TNC to participate test phase, TNC help model learn discriminative feature for final classification task. This is especially useful when the number of labes is very small (e.g., CIFAR-10 with 10 labels shown in Tab.1).

- Although we use the hard label to train TNC described in Sec. 3.2, we enforce consistency regularization on TNC with soft label. This ensures that TNC can recieve mult-class information to help model learning better data representation of unlabeled data  from the aspect of "what is it not". Additionaly, our experiments find that the class of $\arg\min (p^w)$  changes in the early stage of TNC training, which also allows TNC to learn various complementary labels.

- This design is based on the consideration of it’s unreasonable to directly involve complementary label based negative learning in semi-supervised. In the early training stage of semi-supervised learning, the accuracy of pseudo-labels is often not very high.  In this process, the introduction of complementary labels directly into the learning process will not only be helpful, but even harmful, and lead to training collapse finally. To demonstrate this, we conduct additional ablation studies on TNC in revision, which can be found in Sec. D.3.


>Q2. From the Table 1, the numbers seem pretty strong. However, the variance of the reported accuracies for CIFAR-10 with 10 labels is very high. Although the absolute difference is ~10%, the variance is also ~10%, which requires further explanation.

This situation is caused by too few labels. If only one label is used for each class, the performance of the semi-supervised learning algorithm will be unstable. Model performance will be severely affected by the quality of labeled data. The quality of labeled data selected by different random seeds can lead to very variable results. The same discussion can be found in Sec. 4.4 in [1].

>Q3. Similarly, on CIFAR-10 with 40 and 80 labels as well as CIFAR-100 with 200 labels, the difference of accuracy between the next best method (CoMatch) and MutexMatch is marginal (93% vs 93.4%, 94% vs 94.3%)and often equivalent to the reported variance (0.2% and 0.8%). (It is completely fine with me if your method is not SOTA, but the high variance requires some explanation).

The variance of results on CIFAR-100 with 200 labels is similar to CIFAR-10 with 10. Too few labels will lead to high variance because the quality of labeled data will affect performance significantly in this scenario. 

CoMatch integrated the ideas of consistency regularization, entropy minimization, contrastive learning, distribution alignment, and graph-based SSL in a unified framework, and jointly train two contrastive representations on unlabeled data and smooth the pseudo-labels under the help of a large memory bank. Besides, the success of CoMatch is also based on a strong assumption *"the labeled data and unlabeled data share the same class-distribution"* Our method overcomes the above limitations and still achieves competitive performance.

>Q4. Figure 9 is not present in sec 5.2. Did you mean Fig 7?

Thank you for pointing out our mistake, we have fixed this typo in the revision.

>Q5. From fig 7a,b,c, it seems that the difference between various ways of training TNC give roughly the same result. So the take-home message of this whole ablation seems pretty weak to me.

We carefully design the training scheme of TNC. In Fig. 7, other training schemes will degrade the performance of the model to a certain extent, and the accuracy of their pseudo-labels and complementary pseudo-labels is not very stable.

content.title: Response to Reviewer y2Kv (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank for your detailed feedback! We feel sorry our response causes any confusion. Below we give some further explanations.
> Q1) Your argument doesn't really answer my question on is it valid to enforce consistency on TNC outputs. What would it achieve? The figure you show in Fig4 - where a horse image is possibly predicted as multiple other classes can also be achieved by a random classifier. What exactly did enforcing the consistency on TNC outputs achieve? The intuition itself is unclear to me.

We update the Sec. D.3 in revision to explain this question. Please read this section for details. Here we give a brief explanation.

In TPC, we usually adopt the loss calculated on its hard label. That is to say, we penalize an incorrect classification no matter its confidence on its prediction. This paradigm, widely used in previous works, owns its risk of making training process being unstable especially when the label scarcity in labeled samples. Being aware of this, we notice this constraint could be more smooth from the opposite direction. If we can exclude “what it is not”using smooth label (soft label used in consistency regularization on TNC), we can gradually approximate to its actual label, i.e., what it is. This could.be realized by our constraints on the consistency between different weak and strong augmentation. 

Given two augmented variants derived from the same unlabeled instance, we claim that the class probability distributions, (i.e., soft-labels) of their complementary predictions (i.e., the TNC’s outputs) should be consistent. With the help of an independent training process of TNC, the model can be more confident on “what it is not”. As a result, such prediction consistency on TNC can effectively decrease the False-Negative probability in TPC’s predictions. 
Encouraging a similar prediction on strongly augmented variants of unlabled data can help the model to learn more discriminative features. It can in turn affect the TPC’s prediction, such that the False-Negative probabilities can be effectively decreased. Consequently, the True-Positive probability in TPC’s predictions is enlarged. 

e.g., we denote a $1\times 5$ prediction vector outputted by TPC as $p$, $p=(0.6,0.2,0.05,0.05,0.1)$, the index of the True-Positive component in $p$ is $1$, we use regularization on TNC to encourage TPC (they share the same backbone, TNC encourage model to be more confident on “what it is not”) compress the probability of False-Negative components in prediction vector, e.g.,  $(0.6,0.2,0.05,0.05,0.1)-> (0.9,0.03,0.03,0.02,0.02)$.

A graphical explanation can be found in Fig. 10 in Sec. D.3. We conduct experiments to prove our idea, which is shown in Fig.11 in Sec. D.3.
>Q2,Q3) Thanks for clarifying this. I agree that experiments with fewer labels invariably result in high variance. In this light, I think you should qualify your claims regarding achieving SOTA with 10 labels on CIFAR-10 and 200 labels on CIFAR-100. Also, is the sample selection equal for all the baselines? I mean, are the same 10 labels used for all the baselines for a particular seed?

Thank you very much for your reply. Your understanding is correct and we agree with you. Additionally, we used the same random seeds in our experiments.

>Q5) I think the accuracy of the pseudo-labels and complementary pseudo-labels is not that unstable. If you look at Fig 7c, the y-axis scale is really between 99.4 - 100% - which is reasonably close. Same with 7b. So really this whole ablation is still not clear to me. What correlations do you want to draw from Fig 7b,c to your final accuracies?

We feel sorry  for statements that may cause confusion. The main purpose of the ablation study shown in Figure 7 is to verify the following point: in different training schemes, the accuracy of complementary labels is very high (Fig. 7c), but only by using the default training scheme (Hard-Soft) can we better use consistency regularization on TNC to help the model learn unlabeled data with low confidence. Thereby consistency regularization on TNC can affect the accuracy of pseudo-labels and improve model performance. This can be proved by Fig. 7a, other training schemes lead to performance degradation to the level of FixMatch (88.61$\pm$3.35\% accuracy). Our training scheme (Hard-Soft) is beneficial to consistency regularization on TNC, thereby helping improve performance.

content.title: Response to reviewer y2Kv (2/2)
content.comment:
>Q6. From fig 7c, the complementary pseudo label accuracy seems low for Rev-Norm while the overall accuracy in fig 7a seems almost equal. This raises the question if the complementary accuracy and original accuracy have any correlation at all on this dataset?

This phenomenon is caused by the nature of complementary pseudo-labels. It is easy for us to obtain complementary pseudo-labels with high accuracy. Complementary pseudo-labels with high accuracy are more beneficial for TNC to use mutex-based consistency to help the model learn better data representation of unlabeled data, but its correlation with model performance is not as strong as pseudo-labels.

>Q7. Can the authors provide an ablation into the effectiveness of losses Lp and Ln from eq 1? By not using one or both of lambda_p and lambda_n, what would be the drop in performance? The ablation provided in Fig 9 in the supplementary seems odd to me. lambda_n is varies between 1-20 while lambda_sep is varies between 0.25-1.00, although the losses seem to be roughly of the same scale. A better ablation of the hyperparameters is needed to really distill the effectiveness of the proposed losses.

Your comments are very reasonable and we are happy to add more extensive ablation studies to revision based on your suggestions. More ablation studies on the effectiveness of losses $\mathcal{L_p}$ and $\mathcal{L_n}$   can be in Sec. D.3. 

- $\lambda_{n}=0$. Taking into account that in the default MutexMatch, training of TNC with complementary pseudo-labels stops the gradient, so if we set $\lambda_{n}=0$, then TNC is equivalent to not participating in the training of the model at all, which means that MutexMatch degenerates into FixMatch. So a more reasonable setting is to restore the backpropagation on feature extractor $\theta$ in Eq. 3 to explore the effect of not using consistency regularization on TNC, which is shown in Fig. 10 (*MutexMatch wo. TNC*).  

- $\lambda_{p}=0$. Only use TNC to participate in training, the model will not be able to complete the classification task, which is shown in Fig. 10 (*MutexMatch wo. TPC*).

And more ablation studies on $\lambda_{p}$ and $\lambda_{n}$ are shown in Tab. 8 in Sec. D.2. We conduct experiments varying  $\lambda_{p}$ between 1-20 while $\lambda_{sep}$ varies between 0.25-1.00 because increasing them by a large amount at the same time will result in a large degradation of performance. The same phenomenon occurs when $\lambda_{sep}$， $\lambda_{n}$, $\lambda_{p}$ are greatly increased at the same time, which is shown in Tab. 8 in revision.

Table 8: Accuracy on CIFAR-10 with 40 labels and various $\lambda_{sep}$, $\lambda_{n}$, $\lambda_{sep}$

| $\lambda_{sep}$   | $\lambda_{n}$  | $\lambda_{p}$| Accuracy|
| ----  | ----  |---- |----  |
| 1 |1|1|93.49|
| 1 |1|10|91.27|
| 1 |1|20|85.05|
| 10 |1|1|88.94|
| 20 |1|1|85.44|
| 20 |10|1|18.03|
| 20 |10|10|15.96|

>Q8. It is not really clear what happens at test-time. Do we simply drop the TNC classifier and predict using the TPC network?

Your understanding is correct. We simply drop the TNC classifier and predict using the TPC network because we only use TNC to assist the model to learn better data representation of unlabeled data, TNC did not participate in the testing phase. At the same time, we explored the participation of TNC in the testing phase, which is shown in Fig. 8 in Sec. B.

# References
[1] Kihyuk Sohn, David Berthelot, Chun-Liang Li, Zizhao Zhang, Nicholas Carlini, Ekin D Cubuk, Alex Kurakin, Han Zhang, and Colin Raffel. Fixmatch: Simplifying semisupervised learning with consistency and confidence. In NeurIPS, 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer y2Kv (2/2)
content.comment:
> Q6) You indeed confirm that the correlation of complementary labels with model performance is not as strong as pseudo-labels. So what purpose are they serving?

The accuracy of pseudo-labels is directly related to downstream tasks (classification), while complementary labels are only used to assist us in learning unlabeled data through consistency regularization on TNC. The accuracy of complementary pseudo-labels affects the consistency regularization, which in turn affects the accuracy of the pseudo-labels, and ultimately affects the performance of the model. At the same time, only the training scheme of TNC designed by us can make the consistency regularization work better. The details on this regularization can be found in revised Sec. D.3 and our new response for Q1.

>Q7) Is lambda_p = 0 (Fig. 10 (MutexMatch wo. TPC)) really that bad? In this case, I understand that you would only use the supervised part of the data to train a classifier. What is meant by "the model will not be able to complete the classification task"? I am referring to eq (1). I might not have been very clear with my request, but what I actually asked is the effect of having/not having losses  and . Like (0,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,1,0) combinations of these losses which make sense. It is really expected that values of (20,10,10) will break the training that doesn't tell us much regarding the influence of these losses. Please provide these (or a subset of these) values only if it is not too much of a work in the next few days.

- We apologize for our confusing statement. We have revised the description of this part in Sec. D.3. Your understanding is partially correct. We set $\lambda_{p}=0$ in *MutexMatch wo. TPC*  and use TNC to learn unlabeled data. Notably, TNC is the classifier that finally participates in the testing phase.  For TPC in this case, the training of TPC is indeed equivalent to using only labeled data (i.e., supervised part of the data). Meanwhile, The training of TNC is closely related to TNC (Sec. 3.2). In this case, TNC has not been well trained, too. The reason for  poor performance of this setting is that we use TPC for classification (TNC is used to learn complementary pseudo-labels, in fact, we don't let it participate in the testing phase), and TPC in this case does not get adequate training. i.e., *model (the classifier TPC) can not complete the classification task.* 

- We follow your suggestions and add experiments in our revision which are shown in Fig. 12c and Fig. 12d (denote as MutexMatch w. (0,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,1,0) respectively). The results of experiments prove the necessity of each component in MutexMatch.  More details can be found in revised Sec. D.3.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a framework of semi-supervised learning with mutex-baesd consistency regularization. On top of the framework of consistency-based regularization, the proposed method incorporates a new branch to learn from negative labels. Specifically, it uses a TNC module to predict the class with lowest confidence in TPC and perform consistency regularization for training examples with low confidence. Authors conduct experiments on various datasets to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. They also present an ablation study to show the specific strategies of learning TNC are crucial to the good performance.
content.main_review:
Strengths
1. Semi-supervised learning is an important problem. The proposed framework is well motivated by making good use of all unlabeled data in semi-supervised learning. 
2. Most parts of the paper are clearly written and easy to read. 
3. The ablation study gives empirical evidences for the effectiveness of the proposed method. 

Weaknesses
1. The technical contribution is a bit incremental, since the core idea of utilizing negative labels has already appeared in previous SSL publications such as [1]. Moreover, it’s not clear why and whether the proposed way (involving an extra TNC) to employ negative labels is superior to existing manners such as NCE and BCE. 
2. Improvements on CIFAR-100 are not significant. I wonder whether the algorithm will perform well on datasets with more classes? To my understanding, predicting a specific negative label (the most negative one) sounds not reasonable when there are many classes. 

[1] In defense of pseudolabeling: An uncertainty-aware pseudo-label selection framework for semi-supervised learning. (ICLR’21)
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend weak rejection considering the weaknesses in technical novelty and potential limitations.

content.title: Response to reviewer 7zCe (1/2)
content.comment:
Sincerely thank you for your comments and your effort! We think your comments are very valuable, and we will give some answers to the questions below.

>Q1. The technical contribution is a bit incremental, since the core idea of utilizing negative labels has already appeared in previous SSL publications such as [1]. Moreover, it’s not clear why and whether the proposed way (involving an extra TNC) to employ negative labels is superior to existing manners such as NCE and BCE.

- We are sorry for our confusing statement. Our core idea is utilizing total unlabeled data by mutex-based consistency regularization. Most  existing methods  usually  concentrate on the utilization of high-confidence samples yet seldom fully explore the usage of low-confidence samples like [4], whereas we use TNC to improve this.
In brief, we can’t introduce complementary label to SSL intuitively. We carefully designed the method of using complementary labels. Thus, it can play a positive role in the learning of unlabeled data with low confidence.

- We use TNC to decouple the part where complementary label are directly involved in training. And then enforce consistency regularization on TNC by soft label so as TNC can help model learn a better data representation of unlabeled data. Similar questions about the reason why we use TNC can be found in Q2 of reviewer1 and Q1 of reviewer3, we sincerely hope that you can read our answers under these questions for more explanations. Meanwhile, following your insightful comment, we conduct additional ablation studies on TNC to verify the superiority of the proposed way to utilize complementary label, which can be found in Sec. D.3 in revision.

- And our method of using complementary label is very different from [1] [2]. Moreover, our work is significantly different from [3]. [3] propose an uncertainty-aware pseudo-label selection and negative label is selected when $p_{c}\leq \tau_{n}$, i.e, the confidence is less than threshold. [3] introduces an additional hyper-parameter (another hyper-parameter is $\tau_{p}$ used to select positive labels) to select negative labels whereas we use only one threshold. Additionaly, [3] wastes a part of unlabeled data with $p_{c}$ when 
$\tau_{n}<p_{c}< \tau_{p}$. Furthermore, we use another way to utilize complementary labels which is distinct from [3]. i.e, we use TNC to learn the information of complementary labels which helps model learn a better representation of unlabeled data so as can help model to exclude potential wrong classes for unlabeled data which is illustrated in Fig.1 and we verify our idea in Sec. 4.3. 
Finally, we outperform [3] shown in Tab.2 in Sec. 4.1, which proves the superiority of our way of utilizing complementary pseudo-labels.

content.title: Response to Authors - Round 2
content.comment:
Thank you for the response. It’s much clearer to me that the core idea is in fact to split the consistency regularization into two parts (positive and negative portion). This should be a novel design, different from existing work. Despite this, I still suggest authors to improve the presentation, especially the Introduction part. In the current manuscript, complementary label and TNC are overemphasized. They are actually only tools used to move those unconfident samples to the TNC portion to perform consistency regularization. The second paragraph of the Introduction    is especially misleading (though intuitive and interesting) for understanding the real technical contribution of the paper. Moreover, as the idea of complementary label is not original, there should be citations in this part. 

My second question in Weaknesses.1 is still not solved. To my understanding, the proposed method is built on FixMatch( It’s exactly FixMatch if removing all components linked to TNC). FixMatch (as well as MixMatch) is a combination of pseudo label and consistency regularization. MutexMatch is motivated by the problem that FixMatch wastes those unconfident samples (so you move them to the TNC branch). But why can’t we utilize them in much simpler manners,  e.g. by negative cross-entropy loss (NCE) as suggested in [1]? (It seems easy and straightforward to implement.) To my opinion,  MutexMatch is a bit complicated compared to SOTA methods and I doubt whether such extra modules are indeed necessary. Table 2 is not convincing enough to validate the advantage of TNC, since UPS[1] is evaluated based on the primitive pseudo-labelling method (without mixing consistency regularization) but MutexMatch is based on FixMatch. please correct me if my understanding is incorrect.

[1] In defense of pseudolabeling: An uncertainty-aware pseudo-label selection framework for semi-supervised learning. (ICLR’21)

replying_to: Replying to Response to Authors - Round 2

content.title: Response to reviewer 7zCe- Round 2 （1/2）
content.comment:
We would like to sincerely thank the reviewer for their thorough response! We believe that the good questions will help us in improving our submission. In view of the fact that we cannot modify the submission at this stage, but we give our answer below, thank you for reading. Here we begin with the second question in Weaknesses.1.

> My second question in Weaknesses.1 is still not solved. ……But why can’t we utilize them in much simpler manners, e.g. by negative cross-entropy loss (NCE) as suggested in [1]? (It seems easy and straightforward to implement.) 

Your understanding is correct. We have followed your suggestions and supplemented the following experiments built on the paradigm of FixMatch. The experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10 with 40 labels. Then we give a further discussion on the reason why we don’t utilize samples with NCE.
- We remove TNC and select the positive label and the complementary label like [1]. We introduce NCE to learn information of the complementary label (also in the same way as [1]). This is equivalent to the following setting: keep TPC, for the image $x$, TPC output prediction on a weakly-augmented version of $x$ (denoted as $x_{w}$). Then we select the positive label and the complementary label through the threshold $\tau_{p}$ and $\tau_{n}$ [1]. We enforce consistency regularization between the positive label and strongly-augmented version of $x$ (denoted as $x_{s}$), and then enforce NCE on the complementary label of $x_{w}$ for $x$. We set the same $\tau_{n}=0.05$ as [1]. Then we set $\tau_{p}=0.95$ (same as $\tau$ in MutexMatch), $\tau_{p}=0.7$ (same as $\tau_{p}$ in [1]) for two experiments (denoted as *”F w. NCE (1)”* and *”F w. NCE (2)”* respectively).
- We keep all settings of *”F w. NCE (1)”*. Instead of learning information of complementary label by NCE directly, we enforce consistency regularization between $x_{w}$ and $x_{s}$ by NCE (denoted as *”F w. NCE (3)”*). 

The results of the experiments are shown in Table a.

Table a: Ablation studies on CIFAR-10 with 40 labels.

| Ablation| $\tau_{p}$|$\tau_{n}$|Complementary Pseudo-label Accuarcy| Accuarcy |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| F w. NCE (1)|0.95|0.05|98.84|87.82|
| F w. NCE (2)|0.7|0.05|97.73|78.14|
| F w. NCE (3)|0.95|0.05|98.62|84.33|
| MutexMatch (Hard-Hard)|0.95|-|99.96|90.56|
| MutexMatch|0.95|-|99.91|93.40|

As shown in Tabel a, we can see MutexMatch outperforms other setting utilizing samples with low confidence by simpler manner NCE. We analyze that the direct use of NCE to learn complementary label like [1] will lead to “homogenization” of the learned information. i.e., The CE loss on the positive label and the NCE loss on the complementary label share predictions of the same classifier. Moreover, the probability of the element (corresponding to complementary label selected by the threshold $\tau_n=0.05$) in prediction is very close to 0. The threshold $\tau_n$  is small because [1] needs to ensure the accuracy of the complementary label. In this case, the impact of the loss item of NCE is very small. This way of using low-confidence samples may not be informative, resulting in little help to the model, which means that the final performance is still at the FixMatch level (even lower), which can be confirmed by the results of *”F w. NCE (1)”*, *”F w. NCE (2)”* and *”F w. NCE (3)”* shown in Table a. But even if [1] uses a very small threshold $\tau_n$, the accuracy of the complementary label selected by [1] is lower than that of the complementary label output by TNC in MutexMatch. Considering that [1] treats complementary labels as hard labels, for fair comparison, we also provide the results of *“MutexMatch (Hard-Hard)”* which can be found in Sec. 5.2 (hard complementary pseudo labels are used for separate training of TNC and consistency regularization on TNC).

The ablation study in [1] also demonstrates our claims which is shown in Table. 5 in [1].
*”UPS [1], no NL”* means that UPS removes the component of learning of complementary label (i.e., negative learning by NCE). We can see that the use of negative learning (NL) does not bring significant performance improvement, which proves that the role of NCE in the UPS [1] framework is not significant (NL leads only  0:32% error rate reductions for 4000 samples).

Table 5 in [1]: Ablation Study on CIFAR-10 dataset (Error Rate (%)).

content.title: Response to reviewer 7zCe- Round 2 （1/2）
content.comment:
## Continuation

As we responded for Q1 in your previous comments, we use TNC to decouple the part where complementary label are directly involved in training (separate training of TNC described in Sec. 3.2). i.e., we make the information contained in positive labels and complementary labels “heterogeneous” (by two classifiers with different training schemes), and learn unlabeled data from two different views by mutex-based consistency regularization.

Moreover, the way to use NCE in [1] relies on the use of thresholds to select complementary labels, which means that information of elements beyond the threshold in the classifier's prediction is not used. MutexMatch enforces consistency regularization on TNC by soft label so as TNC can help model learn a better data representation of unlabeled data. i.e., our consistency regularization on the soft complementary labels of low-confidence samples contains more information. This claim can be verified by the result of *”F w. NCE (3)”* in Table a. More details on the regularization can be found in Sec. D.3 in revision and our responses for Q2 of Reviewer1 and Q1 of Reviewer3.

# References

content.title: Response to Authors - Round 3
content.comment:
I appreciate the authors' efforts in answering the questions. It’s good to see that TNC performs much better than NCE in the FixMatch framework. But I’m sorry that I still think this paper needs a further improvement. In my opinion, the paper’s key technical contribution is to introduce a novel component, Consistency Regularization with TNC (CR-TNC),  for utilizing those low-confident samples, rather than to propose a novel SSL framework (MutexMatch = FixMatch + CR-TNC). As a result, the most important effort in experiments should be put in verifying the effectiveness of CR-TNC under various frameworks. Related works about complementary labels and other methods aiming at utilizing low-confident samples should be carefully discussed and compared in experiments. CR-TNC should be compared against them under the same framework. In this sense, most experimental results (Table 1,2,3) are not informative enough to validate the technical contribution of this paper. Also, the selected framework should not be only limited to FixMatch, in order to demonstrate the generality of your method. CR-TNC should be applicable to any framework where pseudo labels are used.

Though authors made some progress in the response and updated paper, more efforts are needed to make the paper satisfactory in both presentations and experiment analysis. I would stick to my original score.

content.title: Response to reviewer 7zCe- Round 2 （2/2)
content.comment:
> Despite this, I still suggest authors to improve the presentation, especially the Introduction part. In the current manuscript, complementary label and TNC are overemphasized. They are actually only tools used to move those unconfident samples to the TNC portion to perform consistency regularization.

We agree with your suggestions, and we are very sorry for the possible misunderstandings caused by the confusing statements in our introduction. As you said, in the introduction, what we want to highlight is indeed how to use mutex-based consistency regularization to make full use of all unlabeled data. Considering that we cannot modify the submission at this stage, we will be happy to improve the presentation of the introduction if the paper is accepted.

> he second paragraph of the Introduction is especially misleading (though intuitive and interesting) for understanding the real technical contribution of the paper. Moreover, as the idea of complementary label is not original, there should be citations in this part.

- In the second paragraph of the introduction, we tried to show an intuitive explanation for implementing consistency regularization on TNC. Further explanation of this regularization can be found in our responses for Q2 of Reviewer1 and Q1 of Reviewer3, and we have added Sec. D.3 in the revision to give what the consistency regularization on TNC has achieved.

- The citations of complementary labels are given in the related work section (Sec. 2), but your suggestion is very reasonable. Considering that we cannot modify the submission at this stage, we will happy be happy to add this citation to the introduction if the paper is accepted.


> To my opinion, MutexMatch is a bit complicated compared to SOTA methods and I doubt whether such extra modules are indeed necessary. Table 2 is not convincing enough to validate the advantage of TNC, since UPS[1] is evaluated based on the primitive pseudo-labelling method (without mixing consistency regularization) but MutexMatch is based on FixMatch. please correct me if my understanding is incorrect.


Our method is based on FixMatch and is simpler than SOTA method CoMatch. CoMatch integrated the ideas of consistency regularization, entropy minimization, contrastive learning, distribution alignment, and graph-based SSL in a unified framework, and jointly train two contrastive representations on unlabeled data and smooth the pseudo-labels under the help of a large memory bank. Besides, the success of CoMatch is also based on a strong assumption "the labeled data and unlabeled data share the same class-distribution". Our method overcomes the above limitations and still achieves competitive performance.  Table 2 is just to show our performance comparison under the same setting as [1]. In addition to Table 2, a comparison with SOTA methods that mix consistency regularization can be found in Table 1. To prove the necessity of each component of our method, we have added new ablation studies into Sec. D.3 in revision, which is shown in Fig. 12.

content.title: Response to reviewer 7zCe (2/2)
content.comment:
>Q2. Improvements on CIFAR-100 are not significant. I wonder whether the algorithm will perform well on datasets with more classes? To my understanding, predicting a specific negative label (the most negative one) sounds not reasonable when there are many classes.

Thank you for the detailed review and thoughtful feedback. We are very sorry for possible misunderstandings caused by not explaining our methods in detail. Your opinion is undoubtedly correct, it is unreasonable to predict a specific negative label (the most negative one) when there are many classes. But we only use *"the most negative one"* generated by TPC to train TNC separately (more details can be found in Sec. 3.2), and the purpose is to ensure that TNC predicts complementary pseudo-labels with high accuracy. We did not involve *"the most negative one"* in our mutex-based consistency regularization. In TNC portion of mutex-based consistency regularization, we use soft labels to train TNC to ensure that it can learn multi-class information to help the model learn better data representation of unlabeled data. Even in the separate training of TNC, our experiment found that in the early stage of training, the class of *"the most negative one"* is constantly changing, which demonstrates that TNC can get the guidance information of multi-class complementary labels. In brief,  the separate training of TNC using *"the most negative one"* is just to obtain a robust classifier that outputs complementary pseudo-labels.

We admit that improvements on CIFAR-100 are not significant. RemixMatch achieved SOTA under the setting of 2500 labels on CIFAR-100, but it uses distribution alignment technique which relies on a strong assumption: *"the labeled data and unlabeled data share the same class-distribution"*. We don't use the prior information of the labeled data, so we are not restricted by this strong assumption. 

# References
[1] Takashi  Ishida,  Gang  Niu,  Weihua  Hu,  and  Masashi  Sugiyama.   Learning  from  complementary labels. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 30, pp. 5639–5649, 2017.

[2] Takashi Ishida, Gang Niu, Aditya Krishna Menon, and Masashi Sugiyama.  Complementary-label learning for arbitrary losses and models.  In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp.2971–2980, 2018.

[3] In defense of pseudo labeling: An uncertainty-aware pseudo-label selection framework for semi-supervised learning. (ICLR’21)

[4] Kihyuk Sohn, David Berthelot, Chun-Liang Li, Zizhao Zhang, Nicholas Carlini, Ekin D Cubuk, Alex Kurakin, Han Zhang, and Colin Raffel. Fixmatch: Simplifying semisupervised learning with consistency and confidence. In NeurIPS, 2020.

display_title: Official Review of Paper957 by Reviewer 3Bqn

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new semi-supervised learning (SSL) method that aims to exploit the low-confident samples to train the model. Compared with existing SSL methods, the proposed method adds a true-negative classifier to classify those low-confident samples as true negatives and further adds a consistency regularization on the true-negative predictions. Experiments show that the proposed method reaches significant improvement over existing methods, especially for the low-label regime.
content.main_review:
The advantages of this paper are as follows.
1) This paper proposes a novel  SSL algorithm by exploiting complementary negative labels. 
2) Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the proposed method by comparing existing ones. 
3) The proposed method significantly extends the state-of-the-art performance. 

The disadvantages of this paper are as follows. 
1) The results shown in Table 1 are impressive and the authors accredit this for the TNC module. However, If a random guess has an accuracy of 90% (10-class classification) for the true-negative classification, how could it bring such great improvement as the signal is not very informative. 
2) What is the effect of the consistency regularization against TNC's predictions. This component seems not studied.
3) Why not report the complete results for FixMatch and CoMatch in Table 1? Considering that the authors have implemented FixMatch and CoMatch and conducted some experiments on them, it should be feasible to report the results for the other experimental settings, but why these results are missing.
4)  Figure 9 in the last paragraph of Section 5 should be Figure 7.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method looks simple yet highly effective. But the explanations for the impressive results are not very convincing and some experimental results are missing. With this consideration, I would recommend weak acceptance.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper957 by Reviewer 3Bqn

content.title: Response to reviewer 3Bqn (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for your thoughtful feedback! Below we address specific questions.
> Q1. The results shown in Table 1 are impressive and the authors accredit this for the TNC module. However, If a random guess has an accuracy of 90% (10-class classification) for the true-negative classification, how could it bring such great improvement as the signal is not very informative.

Thanks for your insightful comments. 
- The help to the model provided by introducing complementary label directly is not very informative, so we enforce stronger regularization on TNC to help model learn more valid information of soft complementary labels. More explanations of this regularization can be found in our response for Q2.
- We have discuss the effectiveness of the TNC in Sec. 4.3. Our key idea is to improve the pseudo-labels indirectly by introducing an auxiliary task based on TNC. The existing SOTA SSL methods only use partial unlabeled data with high-confidence predictions, which cannot sufficiently exploit the unlabeled data like [3]. This motivates us to design a TNC classifier to perform negative training on unlabeled samples with low-confidence predictions that are commonly dropped in existing SSL methods. The TNC is to predict “what it is not”, and it can hardly be wrong for TNC in a multi-classs classification task. as shown in Fig. 7(c), the accuracy of TNC’s prediction will quickly increase to 95%. Such easily correct feature for TNC training can gradually improve the feature learning on low-confidence samples, meanwhile, not introducing much error information. In addition, we also adopt the soft-labels to performance the consistency regularization on TNC, which can further benefit the utilization of low-confidence samples. We provide more experiment results and discussions in D.3 of the appendix. As a result, TNC is very helpful in exploiting the unlabeled data. Thus our methods show better superiority when the number of labels is scarce, as show in Table 1.

-  We expect that TNC can output diversified results at the dataset level, which demonstrates it has learned discriminative information from the aspect of complementary label. So, we use soft labels for consistency regularization on TNC to obtain multi-class information. As shown in Fig. 4, TNC does output multiple results for the same class of sample, indicating "what it is not".  Specially, TNC is more helpful to the model when the  label is scarce because it is difficult for TPC to learn in this scenario.

> Q2. What is the effect of the consistency regularization against TNC's predictions. This component seems not studied.

Your comments are valuable! We would like to follow your guidance and add an ablation experiment for consistency regularization on TNC in the revision, which can be found in Sec. D.3 in appendix.  Here we give a brief explanation for this consistency regularization.

- Given two augmented variants derived from the same unlabeled instance, we claim that the class probability distributions, (i.e., soft-labels) of their complementary predictions (i.e., the TNC’s outputs) should be consistent. With the help of an independent training process of TNC, the model can be more confident on “what it is not”. As a result, such prediction consistency on TNC can effectively decrease the False-Negative probability in TPC’s predictions. 
Encouraging a similar prediction on strongly augmented variants of unlabled data can help the model to learn more discriminative features. It can in turn affect the TPC’s prediction, such that the False-Negative probabilities can be effectively decreased. Consequently, the True-Positive probability in TPC’s predictions is enlarged. 
e.g., we denote a $1\times 5$ prediction vector outputted by TPC as $p$, $p=(0.6,0.2,0.05,0.05,0.1)$, the index of the True-Positive component in $p$ is $1$, we use regularization on TNC to encourage TPC (they share the same model, TNC encourage model to be more confident on “what it is not”) compress the probability of False-Negative components in prediction vector, e.g.,  $(0.6,0.2,0.05,0.05,0.1)-> (0.9,0.03,0.03,0.02,0.02)$.


- We use soft labels to enforce consistency regularization on TNC. This ensures that TNC can recieve mult-class information to help model learning better data representation of unlabeled data with low confidence. 

- It is not very intuitive to introduce learning of complementary pseudo-label into semi-supervised learning. We summarize it as a decoupling design, i.e., we do not allow complementary labels to directly participate in training, but use consistency regularization on TNC to learn data representation of unlabeled data.  We utilize this way to help model learning data representation from the aspect of complementary label, which is more effective when labels are scarce, e.g., CIFAR-10 with 10/20labels.

Similar questions can be found in the Q1 of Reviewer3. We sincerely hope that you can read our answer under this question for more explanations.
